key_insight: Visual language models (VLMs) match or exceed humans at high-level object recognition but exhibit widespread deficits on standardized low- and mid-level visual neuropsychological tests, revealing a gap between semantic competence and basic visual processing.
problem_solved: Identifies and quantifies where current VLMs fail on foundational visual abilities that standard high-level benchmarks miss, showing that strong semantics do not guarantee robust low-/mid-level vision.
method: Applied standardized neuropsychological visual tests to a range of VLMs to probe low-, mid-, and high-level visual functions.
Directly compared VLM performance to human norms on the same tests to reveal relative strengths and weaknesses.
Analyzed results by processing level (low/mid/high) to map specific deficits and preserved capabilities.
impact: Highlights that model evaluation must include basic visual processing checks, not just object-level benchmarks; practitioners should test and mitigate low- and mid-level vision failures before deploying VLMs in real-world visual tasks.
visual_elements: Bar chart comparing human vs VLM accuracy across low-, mid-, and high-level test categories

paper_title: Visual language models show widespread visual deficits on neuropsychological tests
